section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review

text: Abstract
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > Abstract

text: This comprehensive review explores electroless cobalt deposition, an appealing surface modification technique that offers advantages such as uniform coverage on complex geometries and compatibility with diverse substrate materials without external power. The article systematically examines the critical impact of various bath constituents and operational variables on the characteristics of deposited films. It details the roles of the cobalt source, different reducing agents, complexing agents, pH regulators, and stabilizers. Additionally, the article scrutinizes the influence of deposition parameters like temperature, solution pH, agitation methods, and bath aging. The formation of numerous cobalt-based alloys and composite materials are also discussed. This review aims to guide the development of optimized electroless cobalt plating solutions, highlighting their wide-ranging utility in fields such as microelectronics, data storage, protective coatings, electrolytic green H₂ generation metal matrix composites, and electromagnetic shielding, thereby fostering advancements in intricate material fabrication Keywords Electroless Cobalt Protective coating Thin film

text: 1 Introduction
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 1 Introduction

text: Electroless cobalt plating stands out as a versatile and efficient method for depositing a thin layer of cobalt metal on any surface. Unlike traditional electroplating, which relies on external electrical current, electroless cobalt utilizes a chemical reduction process. This eliminates the need for exclusively conducting substrates, complex electrical setup and allows for more uniform deposition on intricate surfaces. The process is steadily gaining traction since its inception by Brenner and Riddell [1] in 1947 due to simplicity of the technique and lower cost of instrumentation. Electroless coating or autocatalytic coating is a category of chemical process that deposits one or more metal layers by autocatalytic reduction of metal cations in a liquid chemical bath. One of the significant advantages of electroless plating is its ability to achieve a more even and conformal coating compared to electroplating. Unlike electroplating, homogeneity of deposit thickness is maintained even in the sharp corners or intricate recesses of the substrate surface [2, 3].
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 1 Introduction

text: This characteristic makes it ideal for applications where uniform coverage is crucial, such as in microelectronics and the fabrication of magnetic thin films. The composition of the electroless plating solution can be tailored to control the properties of the deposited cobalt layer. Electroless cobalt alloy finds applications in various fields. In the microelectronics industry, it is used to create diffusion barriers [4, 5] and seed layers [6, 7] for subsequent electroplating processes. The magnetic properties ofcobalt make it a valuable material for data storage devices and magnetic sensors [8, 9]. Since US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) categorized Cr 6+ containing baths (essential for hard chrome plating) as unsuitable for environment and stressed on alternative approaches [10], cobalt-based plating has also been explored and employed for wear [11–13] and corrosion [14, 15] protection of metallic components. While electroless plating excels at creating thin films, its potential extends far beyond simple flat surfaces.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 1 Introduction

text: Deposition of 3D structures like cobalt microspheres [16, 17] and 1D structures like nanowires [18] or nanotubes [19] has been successfully demonstrated, paving the way for a new generation of micro and nanostructured materials with enhanced functionalities in various fields.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 1 Introduction

text: As research in this area continues, advancements are being made to optimize electroless cobalt plating solutions for specific applications. Although a large volume of research work is available, comprehensive review article on this area is scarce. Shen et al. [20] in 2022 provided a summary on the progress of electroless cobalt deposition narrowly focusing on semiconductor-based electronics application. The main aim of the current article is to discuss and summarize past works on the influence of bath composition and coating parameters on autocatalytic cobalt deposition. The article also includes brief discussion on the development of Co-based alloys and composites structures obtained via electroless path and their intended applications.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 1 Introduction

text: 2 Electroless Cobalt Deposition Process
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 2 Electroless Cobalt Deposition Process

text: The deposition process involves reduction ofcobalt cations in an aqueous solution ofmetal salt in the presence ofa reducing agent (R) at the surface of a catalytic substrate. Deposition then continues due to the catalytic action of the deposited metal ions. Hence, the process is also named as autocatalytic. In the course of time, four different detailed reaction mechanisms were proposed to account for electroless deposition process [21]. Among them, the electrochemical mechanism has been experimentally validated by Hwang et al. [22] specifically in case of cobalt deposition. According to this proposition catalyst particles jump start the oxidation (loss of electrons) of reducing agent by acting as anode whereas reduction (gain of electrons) of metal cations happens at a different cathodic site with less catalytic activity. General chemical reaction for the electroless metal deposition process can be expressed as:

text: 2.1 Substrate Pre-treatment
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 2.1 Substrate Pre-treatment

text: Figure 1 shows all the steps needed to be followed for successful deposition. Ensuring the substrate to be clean and free of contaminants like grease, oil, or oxides is of paramount importance in order to obtain good quality deposit. Electroless cobalt deposition thrives on the inherent catalytic nature of the substrate. However, advancements have opened doors to depositing cobalt on non-catalytic substrates as well. Iron, nickel, cobalt, gold, palladium, and aluminum substrates can act as catalysts [23], while non-catalytic substrates such as copper, magnesium, polymers, carbon, glass etc. are activated using PdCl _ 2 solution [23–25] because Pd nanoparticles act as seeds, providing numerous active sites for the cobalt ions to be reduced and initiate the electroless deposition process [26]. Non-catalytic substrates must be sensitized by dipping into stannous chloride ( SnCl _ 2) solution before palladium activation. It effectively prepares the surface by depositing Sn ^ 2 + ions [25, 27]. The adsorbed Sn ^ 2 + ions act as a reducing agent. They donate electrons to the Pd ^ 2 + ions in the solution. As a result, the Pd ^ 2 + ions are reduced to metallic palladium ( Pd ^ 0) [28].
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 2.1 Substrate Pre-treatment

text: However, sensitization can be considered unnecessary when the substrate surface chemistry inherently provides sufficient sites for direct palladium ion adsorption and subsequent reduction to its catalytic metallic form [29, 30]. In an effort to find an activation process without using Pd ^ 2 +, Zhang et al. [31] reported successful use of aluminum foil in conjunction with non-catalytic copper substrate. Mukherjee et al. [32] successfully replicated aluminum induced electroless cobalt alloy deposition on copper foil. Hu et al. [33] demonstrated a method of directly depositing a catalytic cobalt seed layer on a copper substrate using a process called galvanic replacement where a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from an ionic solution.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 2.1 Substrate Pre-treatment

text: 2.2 Bath Preparation and Deposition
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 2.2 Bath Preparation and Deposition

text: The aqueous bath primarily consists of a cobalt salt as the source of cobalt ions, a reducing agent to convert cobalt cations to cobalt atoms, complexing agent, pH regulator, and stabilizer. The prepared solution is heated and maintained at certain temperature, and activated substrate is immersed in the heated solution for deposition. Deposition process can take time ranging from few minutes to few hours depending on the required yield. Schematic diagram of instrumentation is shown in Fig. 2a. Figure 2b shows the electrochemical reaction scheme at the vicinity of the substrate. The effectiveness of the electroless deposition process, which involves heating the solution and immersing an activated substrate, is intrinsically linked to the chemical makeup of the aqueous bath. The specific constituents, including the cobalt salt, reducing agent, complexing agent, stabilizer, are paramount in dictating the deposition characteristics. Understanding these individual components is therefore essential for optimizing the electroless cobalt deposition.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 2.2 Bath Preparation and Deposition

text: 3 Electroless Co Bath Composition
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3 Electroless Co Bath Composition

text: 3.1 Cobalt Source
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.1 Cobalt Source

text: Cobalt (II) salts like cobalt chloride (CoCl) and cobalt sulfate (CoSO_4) are most preferred sources of cobalt ions for depositing Co-based coatings. Deposition rate is slightly higher from sulfate bath than chloride bath [34]. Brenner and Riddell reported that more than 0.17 M Co salt in the bath results in darkening of coating with significantly lower deposition rate [23]. According to the findings of Magagnin et al. [5], 0.1 M cobalt sulfate results maximum deposition; then, the yield decreases. Consequently, usual practice is to keep the concentration of Co salt within 0.1 M. Although no other report is available for successful reduction of Co (III) salts, Djokic [35] in 1998 claimed to have successfully reduced hexamine cobalt sulfate ( [Co(NH_3)_6]_2(SO_4)_3) into elemental cobalt using hydrazine as reducing agent.

text: 3.2 Reducing Agent
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.2 Reducing Agent

text: Reducing agent is the primary driving force for the electroless deposition reaction. They donate electrons to the metal ions in the plating solution. As the metal ions receive electrons, they are reduced to their metallic state. An effective reducing agent must contain two or more reactive hydrogen atoms as it is observed that metal ions are reduced to neutral atoms by autocatalytic dehydrogenation of the reducing agent [21]. Reducing agent can be classified into three different groups depending upon the resulting deposit—P containing reagents, B containing reagents and reagent which yields pure Co. The catalytic activity of the seed layer depends on the reducing agent. For optimal electroless plating, the potential ofcatalyst metal to reach a reference current density ( 1 × 1 0 ^- 4 A. cm ^- 2 [36]) should be slightly more positive than the standard reduction potential of the reductant. Ohno et al. [36, 37] evaluated and summarized the catalytic activity of different metals in the presence of different reducing agents. Different reducing agents with different compositional yields and corresponding catalytic activity of different metals are furnished in Table 1.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.2 Reducing Agent

text: The role of sodium hypophosphite ( NaH _2 PO _2·H_2 O) has been widely investigated. Brenner et al. [23] initially reported negligible Co deposition at hypophosphite concentration of 0.1 M or less, while increasing concentration of hypophosphite increases deposition rate. Tarozait et al. [38] observed that increase of hypophosphite concentration up to 0.5 M increases the deposition rate of Co on substrate, with further increase in concentration, deposition rate increases very slightly. Magagnin et al. [5] reported maximum deposition rate at 1.5 M hypophosphite concentration, and further increase drastically reduces the deposition yield. Stoychev et al. [39] also found similar pattern of increasing, reaching a peak and then drastic fall of deposition rate with increasing hypophosphite concentration. text: Use of sodium hypophosphite causes incorporation of P in the cobalt matrix. Miksic et al. [40] provided the earliest report on the amount of P present in Co matrix deposited with different hypophosphite concentration. They found that increasing hypophosphite concentration from 0.047 M to 0.24 M resulted in an increase of the P content from 0.5% to 2.5%. Frieze et al. [41] varied the hypophosphite concentration within slightly wider range (0.05 M to 0.5 M). They were able to increase the amount of P from 1% to 5%. Schlesinger et al. [42] obtained Co-P deposits with the amount of P ranging from 3% to 12% and found almost linear relationship between P content and hypophosphite concentration. They also conclusively observed the tendency of decreasing grain size with increasing amount ofP which was previously hinted by the observations of Cortijo et al. [43]. During nucleation and subsequent growth of Co film on the substrate surface, P atoms act as growth inhibitor resulting in smaller grain size [41, 44].

text: Among boron containing reducing agents, Pearlstein et al. [47] initially investigated the role of DMAB as reducing agent and observed linear increase of deposition rate with increasing DMAB concentration up to 0.07 M. They were able to incorporate maximum of 1.7% B in the Co matrix resulting in a bright and smooth deposit. Addition of further DMAB caused rapid bath decomposition. Saito et al. [48] and Rohan et al. [49] also independently observed linear relationship between deposition rate and concentration of DMAB in the bath. Additionally, Saito et al. [48] reported that amount of B reaches at its peak at 0.075 M DMAB concentration. It is noteworthy that DMAB loses electrons more readily than Co at the vicinity of Cu substrate. Because of this Co can directly be reduced on the otherwise non-catalytic Cu surface without any pre-activation [50]. Morpholine borane (MB) acts in a similar manner as DMAB [51]. text: 3.3 Complexing Agents
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.3 Complexing Agents

text: The complexing agent binds with cobalt ions ( Co 2 ^+) in the solution, forming meta-stable complexes [56]. This reduces the concentration of free cobalt ions available for immediate deposition. This controlled release of free cobalt ions help regulate the deposition rate and prevents uncontrolled precipitation of cobalt. By controlling the availability of free cobalt ions, the complexing agent promotes a more even deposition process across the substrate surface. This leads to smoother and more uniform cobalt films with better adherence to the substrate. The complexing agent used in electroless cobalt bath is usually either an organic acid (Citric acid, tartaric acid, succinic acid, malonic acid, glycine, EDTA etc.) or its salt. Cobalt complex formation is depicted in Fig. 4.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.3 Complexing Agents

text: Brenner and Riddell [23] compared citrate and tartarate salts and concluded that the former produces superior and less porous film than the latter. Pearlstein et al. [47] showed successful use of succinate salt but more than 0.037 M was needed to ensure bath stability. Homma et al. [57] used sodium malonate, a salt of malonic acid, as complexing agent to obtain Co-P film with preferential crystal orientation in perpendicular direction. Saito et al. [48] compared four different complexing agents namely succinic acid and sodium salts of tarataric, citric, and malonic acid in a Co-B bath. In all cases, deposition rates are almost constant up to a certain concentration of complexing agent, beyond which the deposition rate gradually decreases. Higher deposition rates were obtained from succinic acid bath and sodium malonate bath compared to other two. Apart from sodium tartarate, other three complexing agents do not influence B content in the deposit in any significant way. Addition of sodium tartarate favors the amount of B in the deposit. Tarozait et al.

text: [38] explored the role of glycine in electroless Co-P formation and found that deposition rate initially increases with glycine concentration, reaches a peak and then diminishes. They also observed the negative effect of glycine in incorporating P in the Co matrix. Later, it is reported that glycine concentration in between 0.6 M and 0.8 M can be used to achieve directional crystal growth of Co-B, more than that retards the process [51]. EDTA (Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) [58] and ethylenediamine [59] are also reported to be useful as complexing agents. Ethylenediamine reportedly can be used as complexing agent in conjunction with trace amount of diethylenetriamine or triethylenetetramine to deposit Co-B from DMAB bath without any prior need of Pd activation [60]. Diethylenetriamene also enable the bath to accommodate higher DMAB concentration without premature decomposition [58, 60].

One of the major differences between the composition of electroless Ni and Co bath arises from the fact that addition of ammonium salts in electroless Ni baths does not bring forth any kind of significant change while in Co bath it behaves differently. It was well observed from the beginning that presence of ammonia in the bath noticeably increases the quality of the deposit as well as the deposition rate especially in citrate baths [47, 61]. text: 3.5 Stabilizer
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.5 Stabilizer

text: A Co plating bath can spontaneously decompose at any time which is indicated by increased volume of hydrogen gas evolution. To prevent it from happening trace amount of stabilizer such as thiourea can be used, Addition ofup to 0.3 mg/l increases deposition rate, more than that ensues rapid fall of deposition rate [66]. Trace amount of tyrosene [67] or 0.01 M maleic acid [68] can also reportedly stabilize the bath even for prolonged duration of deposition.

text: 3.6 pH Regulator
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.6 pH Regulator

text: NH OH [9, 23, 40], NaOH [24, 53], or KOH [50] are used as pH regulators for alkaline baths and H_2 SO _4 [47] or acetic acid [60] for acid baths. pH regulator is added continuously to maintain certain predetermined pH level throughout the process. At a pH below 9, the presence of ammonia does not affect the deposition rate of Co-B. However, when the pH is raised above 9 adding NaOH, the deposition rate decreases but addition of NH_4OH to raise the pH above 9 maintains a high deposition rate [69]. In order to avoid alkaline metal or foul-smelling ammonium hydroxide, Tarozaite et al. [51] successfully employed tetramethylammonium hydroxide for alkaline baths.

text: 3.7 Other Additives
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.7 Other Additives

text: Wetting agents, also known as surfactants, are generally used to improve the wettability of a substrate by reducing its surface tension. This allows the electroless bath solution to make better contact with the entire surface, leading to more uniform deposition. Although use of surfactants is not very common in electroless cobalt bath, sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) has been reportedly used in some cases where deposition was done on polyethylene terephthalate [24] or boron nitride substrate [70].
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.7 Other Additives

text: Accelerators enhance the deposition rate on a substrate. They can be categorized into two types. The first type is an accelerator solution into which an activated substrate is dipped before being placed in an electroless bath. The second type is an accelerator that can be added directly to the electroless bath in small quantities. NH_4OH, NaOH, H_2 SO _4 etc. fall in the first category. Osaka et al. [71] compared the accelerating effects of 1 M NH_4OH, 1 M NaOH, and 1.1 2MH_2SO_4 during deposition of C o - P. NaOH reportedly demonstrated maximum accelerating effect although the differences between them were found to be small. Shen et al. [72] found that addition of triethanolamine (TEA) directly into a hydrazine bath as an accelerator enhanced the deposi tion rate of pure cobalt up to five times. TEA forms a complex with cobalt ions in the bath which is believed to be more easily reduced. Trace amount (up to ~ 0.01 mMol) of thiourea in the bath can also be considered as accelerator as it can increase the deposition rate [66, 73].

section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4 Electroless Co Deposition Parameters

text: 4.1 Temperature
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.1 Temperature

text: Electroless deposition is possible at room temperature ( 2 5 - 4 0 ~ ^° C) [55, 74]. With increasing temperature, the deposition rate of metal ions increases almost linearly [75–77]. Figure 5b shows the plot of film thickness versus plating time in different bath temperature. From the plot, it is clearly evident that higher the temperature, lesser the needed time to attain a certain film thickness. Although it can be assumed that still higher deposition rate is possible at temperature more than 9 0 ^° C, maintaining pH at this high temperature is very difficult. Hence, 70–90\^°C is found to be the ideal range of bath temperature for electroless cobalt plating. Generally, increasing the bath temperature accelerates the deposition rate because higher temperatures promote faster chemical reactions and increase the diffusion rates of ions to the substrate surface. However, excessively high temperatures can lead to bath instability and spontaneous decomposition. Optimal temperature control is thus crucial for achieving desired plating kinetics and obtaining uniform, dense, and welladhered coatings. Rahman et al.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.1 Temperature

text: [75] observed that at higher temperature, P content seems to increase in deposited Co-P layer contradicting the earlier claim of Liu et al. [77] who found no dependence of amount of P in the deposit on bath temperature.

Equations 3–5 also indicate that higher pH values (i.e., higher OH− concentration) favor cobalt deposition, an observation consistent with findings in electroless nickel plating [79]. Later, it was found that the variation of deposition rate with pH was heavily influenced by the concentration and the type of the complexing agent. As can be seen in Fig. 6a, in alkaline ammoniacal tartarate bath, higher pH favors deposition rate whereas in alkaline non-ammoniacal citrate bath, deposition rate peaks at around pH 7.5–8 and then gradually diminishes. In alkaline citrate bath with low complexing agent concentration (~ 30 g/l), deposition rate peaks at pH 7.8 but with high concentration (~ 100 g/l) of complexing agent, highest deposition rate can be observed at pH 8.5 [80]. Yu et al. [81] observed when Rochelle salt (potassium sodium tartrate) is employed as a complexing agent, the deposition rate initially rises with increasing pH, peaking around pH 10. For optimum deposition rate of Co-P, pH should be kept in between 8 and 10.

Increasing pH of an acidic DMAB bath from 3.5 to 5 significantly improves deposition rate although at pH 5.5 the bath quickly degrades [47]. Reports on the effect of pH on the amount of P inclusion in the deposit matrix are conflicting. While Chow et al. [44] reportedly observed decreasing P in the matrix with increasing pH, Tarozait et al. [38] observed slight increase in the amount of P inclusion for the same. As discussed earlier in case of deposition rate, here also the differences may arise from the variation in addition of complexing agent. text: 4.3 Ultrasonication and Stirring
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.3 Ultrasonication and Stirring

text: In electroless plating, both ultrasonication and stirring serve the same overall purpose, which is to ensure a uniform and high-quality metal deposition on the surface of the object being plated. Ultrasonication uses high-frequency sound waves to create microscopic vibrations in the solution to dislodge gas bubbles and enhance mass transfer [82]. In electroless Co-P plating, particularly in solutions with low cobalt sulfate concentration as fewer cobalt ions available, the diffusion process becomes more critical for maintaining a steady supply of ions to the substrate surface. The ability of ultrasonication to improve diffusion has a greater impact on accelerating the deposition rate in such scenarios [64]. Ultrasound irradiation reduces the activation energy of the electroless deposition reaction. This essentially means the reaction requires less energy to occur, allowing for a comparable deposition rate at a lower temperature [83]. The mechanism behind this improvement is attributed to ultrasonic cavitation.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.3 Ultrasonication and Stirring

text: The collapse of cavitation bubbles on the solid surface generates micro-jets which effectively clean the catalytic surface by removing contaminants leading to a larger active surface area for catalysis [84]. Yu et al. [85] found that at high ultrasonication power (100 W), the film exhibits cracks on the surface. This is likely because excessive agitation disrupts the film growth process, leading to weak bonding between the deposited particles and creating cracks. They recommend 90 W for deposition of relatively smaller and more regular shaped crystallites.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.3 Ultrasonication and Stirring

text: A linear increase in film thickness is observed with a rise in stirring rate. In order to investigate the effect of stirring, Kim et al. [86] deposited Co-W–P film in different stirring speeds. They found that after 60 s of deposition, the obtained film at rest (0 rpm) is only 50 nm thick, while the film deposited with strong agitation (1280 rpm) reaches a thickness of92 nm implying increased reaction rate at higher stirring speed.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.3 Ultrasonication and Stirring

text: 4.4 Bath Aging
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.4 Bath Aging

text: Ammonia free alkaline cobalt baths do not show any decrease in deposition rate with aging. Alkaline ammoniacal cobalt bath has short span of deposition life due to dissolution of atmospheric oxygen. The bath ceases to provide significant deposition after 240 min of aging time. Continuous charging of nitrogen gas can prevent this kind of deterioration [63]. Thermally treating the bath by increasing its temperature to 20~^°C higher than operating temperature, keeping there for 45 min and then cooling it back to operating temperature can also reportedly rejuvenate the solution [87]. Various types of electroless cobalt-based deposition baths, including Co-P, Co-B, and pure Co, have been developed. A comprehensive overview ofthe different bath formulations and their resulting deposit compositions is presented in Table 2, providing a valuable resource for researchers and engineers in this field.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.4 Bath Aging

text: 5 Electroless Co Alloys with Other Metals
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 5 Electroless Co Alloys with Other Metals

text: Apart from hydrazine baths, all electroless Co baths yield binary alloys with either P or B depending on the reducing agent present in the solution. During earlier decades of electroless cobalt research Pearlstein et al. [88] observed that it is possible to produce cobalt alloys by adding other metal salts in the ammoniacal Co-P bath. Although addition of stannate ( SnO _ 3 ^ 2 -) ions fail to produce zinc or tin alloy of cobalt, adding nickel, tungstate, rhenium, or ferrous ions readily produces Ni, W, Re, or Fe alloys of Cobalt. In the following years several binary (Co–Ni [89], Co–Re [90], Co–Sn [32], Co–Fe [91] etc.), ternary (Co–Ni–P [92, 93], Co–W–P [65], Co–Ni–B [94, 95], Co–W–B [50], Co–Fe–P [96], Co–Fe–B [73], Co–Zn–P [97], Co–Mo–P [98], Co–Mo–B [53], Co–Re–P [99], Co–Re–B [100] etc.), and quaternary (Co–Ni–Re–P [99, 101], Co–W–Zn–P [102] etc.) alloys with other metals have been developed. In contrast with the findings of Pearlstein et al. [88], C o - Z n - P was developed by Zheng et al. [97] by adding ZnSO_4 as Zn precursor in the Co–P bath.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 5 Electroless Co Alloys with Other Metals

text: Electroless Co–Sn was developed using SnCl as Sn ^ 2 + source [32] but no report is available for successful use of \SnO _ 3 ^ 2 - as Sn precursor. Addition of Ni ^ 2 + [ 9 2 ] or Z n ^ 2 + [97] to the bath suppresses the reduction of Co ^ 2 +, and promotes the amount of Ni or Zn in the deposit at the expense of cobalt. Co–Ni or Co–W-based alloys are the most explored ones. In case of Co–Ni-P alloys, within pH range 8.0–9.0 rising pH seems to favor Ni content in the alloy [92] but pH 10 or more favors the amount of Co in the deposit [103]. It is noted that addition of even small amount of Ni salt significantly increases the deposition rate and in general favors Ni content in the deposit [104]. Presence of sodium tungstate ( Na _2 WO _4) in Co bath produces Co-W alloy. While use of hypophosphite as reducing agent produces Co-W–P alloys [105], use of DMAB or borohydride yields Co-W-B alloys [106] and using both hypophosphite and DMAB can result in Co-W–P-B alloy [107]. Various electroless Co ternary alloy baths are furnished in Table 3.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 5 Electroless Co Alloys with Other Metals

text: 6 Electroless Co 0D and 1D Structures
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 6 Electroless Co 0D and 1D Structures

text: Electroless process is capable to create structures other than spherical grained thin films of Co-P (Fig. 7a) or Co-B (Fig. 7b) on flat surface. Zero-dimensional (0-D) Co nanoparticles (Fig. 7c) can be obtained via electroless route from a bath prepared by dissolving cobalt acetate tetrahydrate in boiling ( 1 5 0 - 1 6 5 ~ ^° C) caustic propylene glycol (C_3H_8O_2) Without any nucleating agent, Co nanoparticles with a diameter of150–400 nm are formed. Addition ofnucleating agents like silver nitrate ( AgNO _3), palladium chloride (PdCl 2), or chloroplatinic acid (H_2PtCl_6) significantly reduces particle size (40–120 nm) [109]. H_2 PtCl _6 can act as a catalyst and enables the formation of metallic Co nanoparticles from hydrazine-propylene glycol bath at room temperature [74]. Yagi et al. [89]produced Co–Ni alloy nanoparticles by adding NiCl 2 in the aforementioned hydrazine-propylene glycol Co bath. H_2 PtCl _6 provides specific locations for cobalt atoms to deposit on, initiating the formation of small cobalt nanoparticles. It also helps to create a more uniform size distribution for the nanoparticles.

text: 7 Electroless Co composites
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 7 Electroless Co composites

text: Co composites formed from electroless bath can be of two types – Co matrix composite and core shell composite. Evenly dispersing inorganic foreign particles like WS [115], SiC [116], or BN [70] in the electroless Co bath with the help of a surfactant (CTAB or SLS) and then depositing Co from this bath on an activated surface yield Co-WS, Co-SiC, or Co-BN composite films, respectively. In this type of composites, these nano or micron-sized inorganic particles are evenly distributed in the Co film to form metal matrix composites.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 7 Electroless Co composites

text: In case of core shell composites, ceramic particle cores or any fiber can be coated with Co to form the composites. The process scheme is shown in Fig. 8c, and SEM image of a core shell composite is shown in Fig. 8c’. Micron-sized WC particles [117, 118], MgO nanoparticles [119], zirconia alumina (ZTA) composite macroparticles [120], or micronsized hydroxyapatite (HA) particles [121] were activated and immersed in the Co bath to coat each particle with cobalt to, respectively, form Co-WC, Co-MgO, Co-ZTA, or Co-HA core shell composite microspheres. A fibrous material like glass fibers [75, 122], SiC whiskers [123], or multiwall carbon nanotubes (MWCNT) [124] can also be activated and placed in the electroless bath to coat each fiber with cobalt in a similar manner to form core shell composite fibers.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 7 Electroless Co composites

text: 8 Applications
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8 Applications

text: Electroless cobalt, a versatile thin film deposited through a chemical process, boasts a distinct set of properties that have driven its adoption in various established industries. However, recent research is also exploring its potential in exciting new frontiers. Major areas of applications are schematically represented in Fig. 9.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8 Applications

text: 8.1 Traditional Applications
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.1 Traditional Applications

text: 8.1.1 Magnetic Recording
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.1.1 Magnetic Recording

text: Magnetic properties ofelectroless Co films, particularly coercivity, have been extensively studied from the beginning. Coercivity is the ability of a ferromagnetic material to resist external magnetic field without being magnetized. Tuneable coercivity of electroless Co-P combined with ultra-thin nature of the deposited film makes it a candidate of interest for high density magnetic recording medium [8, 9, 78]. Ouchi et al. [125] fabricated CoNiP nanodot arrays shorter than 50 nm with high perpendicular magnetic coercivities, using electroless deposition process (Fig. 10a). This is a crucial property for perpendicular magnetic recording technology to increase storage density. Co-P films are promising for magnetic rotary encoders, enabling magnetization into 2048 magnetic pole pairs with uniform output [126]. This improves resolution and accuracy for angle and displacement measurements.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.1.1 Magnetic Recording

text: 8.1.2 Tribological Applications
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.1.2 Tribological Applications

text: Electroless Co-P deposits typically have a fine-grained structure, which contributes to their low friction coefficients and good wear resistance. However, the wear and friction behavior of the deposit can be further improved by annealing the deposit at an elevated temperature. Annealing causes the metal grains to grow, which results in a more uniform and stronger deposit. Klingenberg et al. [127]reported the microhardness (VHN) of Co-B to be 716 kg-f/mm 2 and of Co-P to be 883 kg-f/mm 2 after heat treatment at 350 °C. Composite coating like Co-SiC can exhibit high hardness even without heat treatment [116]. Self-lubricating Co-WS film (Fig. 10b) with very low coefficient of friction can be produced via electroless route [115]. It is also reported that presence of cobalt in electroless film enhances corrosion resistance in acidic [128] and saline environment [14].

section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2 Emerging Applications

text: 8.2.1 Catalytic Activity
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.1 Catalytic Activity

text: Electrolytic hydrogen generation or "green hydrogen" production is a crucial component of a sustainable energy future.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.1 Catalytic Activity

text: Electrolysis involves the decomposition of water into hydrogen and oxygen gases. The material of the electrodes can affect the rate of hydrogen and oxygen production. Noble metals (Ru and Pt) are often used due to their catalytic properties but they are expensive. Transition metal-based catalysts (Co–B[52], Co-Mo-B [53], Co-P [31, 129], Co-P-B [130] etc.) offer more economical options. Electroless deposition is explored as a promising method for achieving uniform and adherent catalyst layers on electrode surface. Catalytic activity of Co-P significantly depends on phosphorus content, with the coating containing 11 wt% P achieving optimal hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) performance, notably a low overpotential of 98.9 mV at 10 mA cm ^- 2 [131]. Efficiency of Co-P-B catalysts stems from synergistic electronic interactions, where electron transfer from B to Co, often modulated by P, creates active sites and optimizes adsorption capabilities [132, 133].
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.1 Catalytic Activity

text: Whether synthesized as coatings on Ni foam for enhanced hydrogen evolution from ammonia borane [132] and sodium borohydride hydrolysis [134], or as amorphous nanoparticles [133] for overall water splitting, Co-P-B materials demonstrate superior reaction rates, lower activation energies, and excellent stability, making them promising candidates for sustainable hydrogen production. Electron micrograph of Co-coated Ni foam developed for catalytic water splitting is shown in Fig. 10c.

text: 8.2.2 Advanced Finishing and Polishing Applications
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.2 Advanced Finishing and Polishing Applications

text: The ability to form composite coatings with diamond particles on substrates such as plastic balls [138] or polyethylene terephthalate cloth [39] showcases versatility of electroless cobalt in creating magnetic abrasive particles and flexible polishing disks. This is crucial for achieving high-quality surface finishes, which is increasingly important in diverse industries from microelectronics to material processing.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.2 Advanced Finishing and Polishing Applications

text: 8.2.3 Coating of Composite Reinforcements and Ceramic Particles
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.3 Coating of Composite Reinforcements and Ceramic Particles

text: Adding small percentage of micro or nano-sized ceramic particles ( Al _2O_3, SiC, MgO, WC, etc.) to metals can make them stronger and tougher as the hard ceramic particles act like tiny obstacles, making it harder for the metal to deform or break. Poor wettability can be a problem in metal matrix composites. If the metal does not adhere well to the ceramic particles, the composite material will be weaker and more likely to fail. One way to improve wettability is to coat the ceramic particles with a different material. This coating can act as a bridge between the metal and the ceramic, making it easier for the metal matrix to spread out and cover the ceramic particles. In recent decades, cobalt is being proven to be a good choice for coating ceramic particles in metal matrix composites [70, 119, 120]. Nambiar et al. [139] successfully developed aluminum matrix composites reinforced with cobalt-coated carbon nanotubes and Al2024 powder, designed for aircraft and automotive applications.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.3 Coating of Composite Reinforcements and Ceramic Particles

text: A crucial finding was that a 10 µm electroless cobalt coating thickness was essential for maintaining reinforcement integrity and preventing defects during fabrication, thereby enhancing composite properties for these uses.

By coating SiC [140], WC [136, 141–143], or WC–Co [144–147] powder particles with Ni–P, Co-P, or Ni-Co, desirable features like a more uniform distribution of the binder, higher sintered densities, and improved interfacial bonding can be ensured.

text: 8.2.4 Electromagnetic Shielding Applications
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.4 Electromagnetic Shielding Applications

text: The ability to deposit uniform and compact cobalt layers on substrates like fibers and microspheres, combined with inherent magnetic properties, makes them ideal for creating conductive fillers for polymer composites. This is crucial for developing flexible and lightweight electromagnetic shield ing materials, which are increasingly vital for protecting sensitive electronics from interference and ensuring data integrity in an increasingly pervasive electronic environment. With reported volume resistivities as low as 4.2 × 1 0 ^- 3 - cm on glass fibers [148], electroless cobalt demonstrates excellent electrical conductivity comparable to or exceeding that of electroless copper ( 6.6 3 × 1 0 ^- 3 - cm [149] to 0.0010 - cm [150]) and nickel ( 5.5 0 × 1 0 ^- 3 -·cm [151] to 6.2 5 × 1 0 ^- 3 - cm [152]) in similar applications. Notably, this conductivity is not as low as that achieved with electroless silver ( 6.5 4×10^-4Ω· cm) [153]. In sophisticated electromagnetic (EM) absorption systems, the outer matching layer is engineered to progressively align the impedance of the ambient air with that of the internal absorbing material.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.4 Electromagnetic Shielding Applications

text: This design ensures minimal surface reflection, facilitating efficient entry of electromagnetic waves for subsequent absorption by the inner layer. Hollow Ni structures coated with magnetic Co-P [154] and Co-MWCNT composite films [124] are developed to address the need for effective matching layer of EM absorbers. They have the potential to be used in stealth technology.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.4 Electromagnetic Shielding Applications

text: 8.2.5 Diffusion Barrier
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.5 Diffusion Barrier

text: Diffusion barriers (Fig. 10f) are crucial in microelectronic devices to prevent unwanted interdiffusion of atoms between different materials, which can lead to device failure. Electroless Co-P [4, 5, 108], Co-W–P [86, 105, 155], and Co-W-B [50] can be employed as interfacial layer in microelectronic contacts to prevent the inter diffusion of materials such as copper [156] and lead-free solders [5], ensuring the long-term reliability of electronic devices. A minimal 0.1% addition of manganese oxide (MnO) particles to electroless Co also reportedly improves its resistance to electromigration by physically blocking atomic movement [157]. Electroless deposited Co-P-W films, particularly those with over 12% P and 2% W, serve as excellent barrier layers in structures like through-silicon vias [158]. Compared to chloride free Pd activation, a PdCl /HCl-based activation process is noted to yield superior, residue-free deposition for such Co-P-W capping layers [159].
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.5 Diffusion Barrier

text: 8.2.6 Bio-Medical Applications
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.6 Bio-Medical Applications

text: Electroless cobalt, particularly in the form of iron-cobalt (FeCo) plated carbon nanotubes (CNTs), presents significant biomedical potential, notably in cancer thermotherapy where these magnetic CNTs serve as heat providers to selectively eliminate cancer cells [160]. Beyond direct therapeutic uses, cobalt-based catalysts, such as Co-Fe/Al_2O_3 system (Fig. 10h), are also highly effective in environmental health applications like the advanced oxidation-based removal of harmful emerging contaminants, including antibiotics, from polluted water, showcasing a broader contribution to human well-being through cleaner environments [91].
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.6 Bio-Medical Applications

text: 8.2.7 Other Microelectronics/Electrical Applications
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.7 Other Microelectronics/Electrical Applications

text: Selective electroless cobalt deposition shows promise as a potential replacement for copper in future CMOS devices [59]. Its ability to achieve high selectivity, good film properties, and self-alignment makes it a promising candidate for overcoming the challenges associated with continued device scaling. By enabling bottom-up fill of high aspect ratio features and providing potential benefits in terms of performance and reliability, electroless cobalt could play a significant role in future generations of advanced logic and DRAM technologies [161]. Goel et al.[162] showed that hysteresis loss of grain-oriented high silicon steels, extensively used to manufacture transformer core, can be minimized by applying a coating of Co–Ni-P thin film via electroless route. Yu et al. [163] successfully fabricated thin electroless Co film as flexible electrode for Li–S batteries. This current collector offers advantages over conventional metallic foils, such as aluminum or copper, because it is less dense and exhibits excellent electrical conduction, stemming from its unbroken formation and intimate interface with the electrode material.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.7 Other Microelectronics/Electrical Applications

text: 9 Outlook
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook

text: Electroless cobalt deposition is a versatile technique with significant potential in microelectronics, data storage, corrosion/wear protection, HER catalysis, and nanostructure fabrication. Despite advancements, several areas need further investigation for broader industrial adoption:
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook

text: Enhanced Deposition Rate and Bath Efficiency: A persistent challenge is the low deposition rate and bath efficiency. Future research should focus on novel reducing agents, catalysts, or additives to accelerate kinetics without compromising quality or stability.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook

text: Tailoring Deposit Properties: More in-depth studies are needed to precisely tailor magnetic, mechanical, anticorrosion, and catalytic properties of electroless cobalt and its alloys for specialized applications. Understanding relationships between bath chemistry, parameters, microstructure, and performance is crucial.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook

text: Environmentally Friendly Practices: Efforts are vital to develop sustainable plating processes, including nontoxic components, reduced waste, and efficient recycling. Pd-free activation can be a promising step in this direction.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook

text: Advanced Characterization and Modeling: A deeper understanding of nucleation and growth mechanisms is vital. In situ and ex situ characterization, coupled with computational modeling, can provide insights into reaction pathways and film development, leading to more rational bath design.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook

text: Addressing these research directions will advance electroless cobalt deposition, leading to more efficient, versatile, and sustainable coating solutions with enhanced properties for future technological applications.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook

text: 10 Conclusions
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 10 Conclusions

text: Electroless cobalt plating is a versatile technique capable of depositing a wide range of cobalt-based coatings, including pure cobalt and various binary and ternary alloys such as Co-P, Co-B, Co–Ni-P, Co-W–P, and Co-W-B. By carefully adjusting the composition of the plating bath and operating conditions, it is possible to tailor the properties of the deposited coatings to meet specific application requirements. These coatings offer numerous advantages, including improved corrosion and wear resistance, enhanced magnetic information storage capabilities, ability to serve as effective barrier layers against copper diffusion or acting as a catalyst in H generation via electrolysis. While many potential applications have been explored, there is still significant room for further research and development in this area. This review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the electroless cobalt plating process by serving as a valuable resource for information on the various chemical baths and operating conditions employed by previous researchers.
section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 10 Conclusions
